summary: States the problem and lists requirements for a GEOPRIV Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol. Such a protocol would let a device ask a Location Information Server for its location, either as actual coordinates or as a reference. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5687 describes how a device might request its location from a server in its access network. It lists requirements for such a protocol and explains privacy and discovery problems it must address.

subtitle: The problem statement and requirements for a device to request location from its access network.

tldr.problem: A device may need its location for applications, but the access network often holds the information needed to determine it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes scenarios, possible ways to discover a Location Information Server, identifier considerations, and ten requirements for a Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5687 is an Informational problem statement, not a protocol definition. Its discovery and identifier options are presented without consensus or recommendation.

today: RFC 5687 is an Informational RFC published in March 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it states requirements and does not define the protocol.

sections.title: The Location Configuration Problem
sections.content:
The proposed Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol (L7 LCP) would let a device obtain location information from a Location Information Server (LIS) in the access network. The location could be returned directly as Location by Value, or the device could receive a reference to location information, called Location by Reference.

Applications could use the location as input to another protocol, such as Location-to-Service Translation, or include it in Session Initiation Protocol signaling. The RFC does not define how the access network determines the device's location; that depends on link technologies and deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: A device may ask a server in its access network for information about where the device is. It can receive the location itself or a reference that another service can use.

sections.title: Network Scenarios
sections.content:
The document considers fixed-wired access, mobile networks, and wireless access. In a fixed-wired network, a home router or network termination device may sit between the host and the access provider. Such legacy equipment may not be changeable to pass location information to the host.

In a moving network, a laptop may move with a portable antenna, bus, train, or airplane without knowing that its location changed. In a wireless hotspot, the access provider may operate the access point and LIS. These scenarios show why a location request must work across different network layouts and device capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can be behind older home equipment, move without detecting the movement, or connect through a public wireless network. The protocol must account for these different situations.

sections.title: Finding the Location Information Server
sections.content:
A device must discover the LIS before requesting location. The RFC assumes that the LIS is in the local subnet or access network and lists several discovery approaches discussed by the design team. It explicitly says the list does not represent consensus or an IETF recommendation.

  • DHCP: provide the LIS name or address, where the network and devices support it.
  • DNS: identify the access network's domain and look up a service record.
  • Redirect: have a network device redirect requests sent to a registered port.
  • Multicast query: ask on the local link; the method does not work beyond it.
  • Anycast: send the discovery request to an address routed to a nearby LIS.

Whichever method is used, the device needs to verify that the discovered server is authorized, so an attacker cannot pose as the LIS.
sections.plainLanguage: The device needs a reliable way to find the right location server. The RFC lists possible approaches but does not select one, and the device must be able to check that the server is genuine.

sections.title: Identifiers Used to Find a Device's Location
sections.content:
The LIS needs an identifier to look up a device's location. The device must know or learn the identifier, and the LIS must be able to use it directly or indirectly. The identifier also needs security properties: an off-path attacker MUST NOT obtain another device's location, and an on-path attacker in the same subnet SHOULD NOT be able to impersonate another device.

The RFC reviews possible identifiers rather than choosing one. A MAC address usually does not travel past one IP hop. A cell identifier may not be visible to the device. An IP address can be useful for returning a response to the requester, but network address translation can hide the device's address, and a shared wireless network can expose location information to an attacker who spoofs an address.
sections.plainLanguage: The server needs a way to tell which device is asking. That identifier must be available to both sides and must not let one user request another device's private location.

sections.title: Ten Requirements for the Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC lists ten requirements, L7-1 through L7-10. The protocol must carry different identifiers or define a suitable mandatory identifier; support a broad range of device mobility; and avoid assuming a business or trust relationship between the application provider and access network provider. It assumes cooperation between the Layer 2 and Layer 3 providers when they are separate.

The protocol must consider legacy equipment, account for VPN awareness, and not assume prior network authentication or knowledge of the access network topology. It must define a mandatory LIS discovery method. When the LIS creates a Presence Information Data Format Location Object, it must place the <geopriv> element inside the <device> element.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements cover different identifiers, mobility, older equipment, VPNs, discovery, and location formatting. They also say the design cannot assume that a device knows the network layout or has already authenticated to the network.

sections.title: Location Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Location information can expose a device and its user to an unauthorized party. The RFC describes four steps for confidential delivery: the client discovers a LIS, authenticates that LIS, the LIS determines and returns the location to an authorized entity, and the messages are exchanged without eavesdropping or tampering.

The discovery process must prevent an attacker from presenting an unauthorized server as the LIS. The identifier must also limit the risk that an attacker requests another device's location. The RFC points to separate GEOPRIV work for a broader discussion of location privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: Location is private information. The device must find and verify the right server, and the request and response must be protected from people who should not see them.

items.title: DHCP
items.text: Can provide the LIS name or address.

items.title: DNS
items.text: Can locate a service record for the access network.

items.title: Redirect
items.text: Can redirect requests to the LIS inside the access network.

items.title: Multicast
items.text: Can query for a server on the local link.

items.title: Anycast
items.text: Can route a request toward a nearby LIS.
